```{r}
library("tidyverse")
library("broom")
library("factoextra")
```

## Loading output data from 03_augment

```{r}
# Load datasets into environment
data_path <- "../data/"


pam50_augmented <- read_tsv(str_c(data_path, 
                                  "03_dat_augment_pam50_filtered.tsv"), 
                                 show_col_types = FALSE)
all_genes_augmented  <- read_tsv(str_c(data_path, 
                                       "03_dat_augment_all_genes.tsv"), 
                             show_col_types = FALSE)
```

# Analysis

## Principal Component Analysis

```{r}
pca_wide <- all_genes_augmented |> 
  filter(`PAM50 mRNA` != "control") |> 
  rename(subtype= `PAM50 mRNA`) |> 
  select(patient_id, subtype, matches("^[NXY]P_"))
```

Using the GeeksForGeeks PCA tutorial listed in the references, we carry out PCA with centering, scaling, and retx.

```{r}
pca_res <- pca_wide |> 
  select(-patient_id, -subtype) |> 
  prcomp(scale.=TRUE, center=TRUE, retx=TRUE)
```

The following two chunks of code will help us observe how much variance is captured by each of the PCs. Then, we will also observe the PC loadings for a couple of proteins.

```{r}
pca_res |> 
  tidy(matrix = "eigenvalues") |>
  slice_head(n=10)
```

```{r}
pca_res |> 
  tidy(matrix = "loadings") |> 
  filter(PC <= 4) |> 
  pivot_wider(names_from = PC, 
              names_prefix = "PC", 
              values_from = value) |> 
  slice_head(n=5)
```

Now, we are plotting the 15 proteins that contribute the most to the first two principal components to observe the direction and the overall contribution of the variables in the PCs.

```{r}
pc_var <- pca_res |> 
  tidy(matrix="eigenvalues") |> 
  mutate(label = str_c("PC", PC, "(", round(percent*100, 1), "%)"))

#Now we extract the labels to avoid using base R
extract_label <- function (pca_n){
  pc_var |> 
    filter(PC == pca_n) |> 
    pull(label)
}

pc1_label <- extract_label(1)
pc2_label <- extract_label(2)

fviz_pca_var(pca_res, select.var = list(contrib=15), repel = TRUE)
```

Finally, we are making a scatterplot colored by subtype to help us answer the if tumors belonging to the same subtype share proteins. If the subtypes properly separate, then we could argue that proteins seem to distinguish the subtypes; whereas if they're all scattered, then the proteins aren't enough to do so. Also, the groups that are placed closer to one another will have similar profiles.

```{r}
pca_scores <- pca_res |> 
  augment(data = pca_wide) |> 
  rename_with(\(x) str_remove(x, "\\.fitted"),
              start_with(".fitted")) |> 
  select(patient_id, 
         subtype, 
         starts_with("PC"))


pca_scores |> 
  ggplot(aes(x=PC1, y=PC2, color = subtype)) +
  geom_point(size=3, alpha=0.8) +
  labs(x = pc1_label, y = pc2_label, color ="PAM50 subtype") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## K-means

Now, we will carry out k-means clustering (with and without PAM50) as a way to further support the answer we obtain after Principal Component Analysis. Right now, we have the PCA scatterplot, which helps us visually observe whether the subtypes are separated properly given their protein profiles, but a K-means will help us back up any conclusion with more numbers. Once again, this is based on a GeeksForGeeks tutorial.

Slight preprocessing to split the protein columns (with and without PAM50).

```{r}
pam50_ids <- read_csv("../data/_raw/PAM50_proteins.csv",
                      show_col_types=FALSE) |> 
  pull(RefSeqProteinID)

pam50_only <- pca_wide |> 
  select(any_of(pam50_ids))

no_pam50 <- pca_wide |> 
  select(-patient_id, -subtype, -any_of(pam50_ids))
```

**Check to see how many proteins survived after the NA filter**

```{r}
ncol(pam50_only)
ncol(no_pam50)
```

Finally, we can carry out the k-means clustering. We are using k = 4 to match the four PAM50 subtypes

```{r}
set.seed(42) #to ensure reproducibility 

kmeans_clust <- function(proteins){
  kmeans(proteins, centers = 4, nstart=20)
}

km_pam50 <- kmeans_clust(pam50_only)
km_nopam50 <- kmeans_clust(no_pam50)
```

We can compare the clusters we obtained with the known subtypes. The next chunks will help us visualize the cluster plots. It is important to mention that this plot will combine both the PC scores together with the results obtained by k-means.

```{r}
pca_kmeans <- pca_scores |> 
  bind_cols(
    augment(km_pam50, pam50_only) |> 
      select(cluster_pam50 = .cluster),
    augment(km_nopam50, no_pam50) |> 
      select(cluster_nopam50 = .cluster)
    )
```

```{r}
pca_kmeans |> 
  count(subtype, cluster_pam50) |> 
  pivot_wider(names_from = cluster_pam50,
              values_from = n,
              values_fill = 0)

pca_kmeans |> 
  count(subtype, cluster_nopam50) |> 
  pivot_wider(names_from = cluster_nopam50,
              values_from = n,
              values_fill=0)

```

```{r}
#Clusters from the PAM50 proteins
pca_kmeans |> 
  ggplot(aes(x=PC1, y=PC2, color = cluster_pam50, shape=subtype)) +
  geom_point(size=3, alpha = 0.8) +
  stat_ellipse(aes(group=cluster_pam50)) +
  labs(title = "K-means clusters (PAM50 proteins)",
       x = pc1_label,
       y= pc2_label,
       color = "K-means (PAM50 proteins)",
       shape = "PAM50 subtype") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
#Clusters for the rest of the proteome minus the PAM50 proteins
pca_kmeans |> 
  ggplot(aes(x=PC1, y=PC2, color = cluster_nopam50, shape=subtype)) +
  geom_point(size=3, alpha = 0.8) +
  stat_ellipse(aes(group = cluster_nopam50)) +
  labs(title = "K-means (without PAM50)",
       x = pc1_label,
       y = pc2_label, 
       color = "K-means (without PAM50)",
       shape = "PAM50 subtype") +
  theme_minimal()
```
